title: Scientific adoption: Established methods persist beside AI
desc: Reports changing method rankings without demonstrating a uniform shift to LLMs or effects on scientific impact.

kps.k: Scientific AI adoption shows changing method rankings alongside persistence of established techniques.
kps.d: The supplied tables from Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus trace frequently adopted methods across scientific fields from 1980–1990 through 2025. Earlier lists feature expert systems and artificial neural networks; several sequences shift from support vector machines in 2011–2015 to convolutional neural networks in 2016–2020. Older methods remain prominent, so the evidence describes evolving method mixes rather than wholesale replacement.

kps.k: Recent rankings do not show a uniform scientific transition to large language models.
kps.d: Entries from 2023–2025 place LLMs alongside CNNs, SVMs, random forests and graph methods. One sequence ranks LLMs third in 2024 and 2025; another ranks them sixth in 2025, while a separate sequence places graph neural networks first in 2023. These differences qualify any account that treats scientific AI adoption as synonymous with LLM adoption. Some excerpts omit field headings, limiting confident assignment of particular rankings to disciplines.

kps.k: The excerpts establish adoption rankings, not AI's effects on scientific impact or research breadth.
kps.d: Despite the paper's title, the supplied material offers no adoption counts, causal analysis or evidence about scientists' impact and the concentration of scientific inquiry. Nor does it present competing arguments, predictions or recommendations. Its practical implication is interpretive: distinguish methods and fields when describing scientific AI uptake, and do not infer comparative performance, productivity gains or narrowing research agendas from frequency rankings alone.

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source supports the proposition directly. Its historical rankings show scientific AI adoption changing by era—most notably from SVM-led rankings toward CNN-led rankings—while established methods continue to appear. Its recent rankings likewise place LLMs within heterogeneous, field-specific method mixes rather than showing a uniform transition to LLMs. Material variation lies across fields and years: LLMs occupy different ranks, and in some sequences CNNs, SVMs or graph neural networks remain ahead. The evidence is limited to adoption rankings, however, so it does not establish adoption volumes, comparative performance, causal effects on scientific impact or changes in research breadth. Because the curated evidence contains only one source in this professional voice, it supports the cluster proposition but cannot establish how broadly this view is held across academia and research.

elens.an: The 2026 source supports the proposition that scientific AI adoption is an evolving, field-specific mix rather than a uniform transition to large language models. Its historical rankings show leadership shifting from support vector machines and artificial neural networks toward convolutional neural networks after 2015, while older techniques remain in use. Its 2023–2025 rankings likewise place LLMs alongside CNNs, SVMs, random forests, transfer learning and graph methods, often below one or more of them. Material variation appears across fields and years: LLMs reach third place in some 2024–2025 sequences, sixth in another 2025 sequence, while graph neural networks lead a separate recent sequence. This variation reinforces the need to distinguish disciplines and methods. The source is narrower than the full proposition in one respect: the supplied tables establish rankings, but provide no adoption counts, causal evidence, comparative-performance findings or evidence about effects on scientific impact or research breadth. Because this time-period facet contains one curated source, these findings characterise that source rather than scientific commentary generally.
